chapter.name: Reshaping India's Political Map
chapter.blurb: Theme B, Tapestry of the Past: how invasions, the Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara, the Mughals and the powers that resisted them redrew India's political boundaries between the 11th and 17th centuries, and how India was administered and lived in through that period.

scope_in.item: The 'medieval' label, the wave of invasions from beyond the Hindu Kush, and the chapter's landmark dates
Rise and fall of the Delhi Sultanate: the five dynasties, Ala-ud-din Khilji, Malik Kafur and Muhammad bin Tughlaq
The plunder economy, iconoclasm, the jizya and Timur's attack on Delhi
Resistance to the Delhi Sultanate: Eastern Gangas, Musunuri Nayakas, Hoysalas, regional sultanates and Rana Kumbha
The Vijayanagara Empire, the Deccan Sultanates and Krishnadevaraya
The Mughals: Babur, Humayun and the Sur interlude, Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan
Aurangzeb: accession, religious policy, the Deccan wars and the strain on the empire
Resistance to the Mughals: Jat peasants, tribal groups, Rani Durgavati, the Rajputs and the Ahoms

Administering India: the sultan and the iqta system, Akbar's ministries, subahs, mansabdari and Todar Mal
People's lives: agriculture, crafts, currency, trade and ports, hundis, temple economies and the stress of the late 1600s

concepts.name: The medieval period and the wave of invasions
concepts.description: What this book means by 'medieval', why invasions from beyond the Hindu Kush reshaped India's political map from the 11th century, and the landmark dates on the chapter's timelines.
concepts.idea: The chapter uses 'medieval' as a borrowed label for the 11th to 17th centuries, a period when an unprecedented run of invasions from outside the Subcontinent redrew India's political boundaries.
concepts.rule: 'Medieval' means 'between two ages' and was originally applied to European history, roughly from the fall of the Roman Empire in the 5th century CE to the Renaissance of the 14th to 16th centuries. Europe's and India's histories are very different and historians do not agree on which Indian period the word covers, so in this book it simply means the 11th to the 17th centuries. From the early 11th century, invasions from beyond the Hindu Kush mountains, mostly by Central Asian Turkic and Afghan peoples, reshaped India's political map; they were drawn by India's reputed riches, by territorial ambition and often by the wish to spread their own versions of their religion by force. Landmark dates include 1206 (Delhi Sultanate), 1326 (Mewar re-established), 1336 (Vijayanagara), 1347 (Bahmani Sultanate), 1398 (Timur attacks Delhi), 1498 (Portuguese arrive), 1526 and 1556 (First and Second Battles of Panipat), 1565 (Talikota), 1576 (Haldighati), 1671 (Saraighat), 1699 (Khalsa formed), 1754 (Maratha control of Delhi) and 1799 (Sikh Empire).
concepts.example: Because the Persian script is hard to transcribe into the Roman script, the same dynasty appears as 'Khalji' in one book and 'Khilji' in another.

concepts.name: Rise and fall of the Delhi Sultanate
concepts.description: The five dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate, its instability and violent successions, the campaigns of Ala-ud-din Khilji and Muhammad bin Tughlaq, the plunder economy, the jizya and Timur's attack.
concepts.idea: The Delhi Sultanate expanded by force but never stabilised: violent successions, plunder-funded campaigns and failed experiments left it shrunken by the time of the Lodis.
concepts.rule: The Delhi Sultanate was formed after the defeat in 1192 of King Prithviraj Chauhan and saw five successive dynasties of Turkic-Afghan origin: the Mamluks or Slave dynasty, the Khiljis, the Tughlaqs, the Sayyids and the Lodis. Successions were usually violent, with almost two sultans out of three seizing power by eliminating their predecessor, so the average reign was hardly more than nine years. Ala-ud-din Khilji raided north and central India, repelled Mongol invasions and sent his slave-general Malik Kafur south. Muhammad bin Tughlaq briefly brought most of the Subcontinent under one ruler for the first time since the Mauryan Empire, but his capital shift to Daulatabad and his token currency both failed. Court wealth came from plunder, taxes and the slave trade; the jizya was levied on non-Muslim subjects; temple images were attacked out of plunder and iconoclasm. Timur's attack on Delhi at the end of the 14th century left the city in ruins, after which the Lodis formed the last dynasty of a much shrunken Sultanate.
concepts.example: Muhammad bin Tughlaq declared cheap copper coins to be tokens worth as much as silver or gold, which encouraged counterfeiting and made the economy decline.

concepts.name: Resistance to the Delhi Sultanate and the rise of regional powers
concepts.description: The Eastern Gangas, the Musunuri Nayakas, the Hoysalas, the breakaway regional sultanates and Rana Kumbha's Mewar, and how their resistance limited Delhi's reach.
concepts.idea: The Delhi Sultanate was checked on every side, by established kingdoms, by local confederacies, by Rajput rulers and by its own governors who declared independence.
concepts.rule: The Eastern Ganga kingdom of Kalinga, covering present-day Odisha and parts of Bengal and Andhra Pradesh, was never subdued; its mid-13th century ruler Narasimhadeva I repelled several Sultanate inroads, defeated the Sultanate's governor of Bengal and built the Surya temple at Konark partly to mark those victories. The Musunuri Nayakas, Telugu chieftains, rallied over 75 more chieftains and expelled Muhammad bin Tughlaq's army from Warangal around 1330 to 1336. The Hoysalas of present-day Karnataka fended off several attacks and remained the only independent kingdom in the south, but weakened by those attacks and by internal conflict they were absorbed into the Vijayanagara Empire in the mid-14th century. Independent regional sultanates broke away, the Bahmani Sultanate controlling much of the Deccan from the mid-14th century, with others in Gujarat and Bengal. In Rajasthan, Rana Kumbha of Mewar offered stiff resistance in the 15th century and built Kumbhalgarh Fort in the Aravalli hills, famous for a wall about 36 kilometres long.
concepts.example: The Hoysalas' name comes from the Kannada story of Sala, who struck a lion to save his guru: 'Hoy (strike)! Sala'.

concepts.name: The Vijayanagara Empire and Krishnadevaraya
concepts.description: The founding of Vijayanagara by Harihara and Bukka Raya, its rivalry with the Bahmani and Deccan Sultanates, the peak reached under Krishnadevaraya, and the destruction of the city after the Battle of Talikota.
concepts.idea: Vijayanagara grew out of a revolt against Delhi's authority into the leading power of the south, and the sack of its capital after Talikota in 1565 ended that role for good.
concepts.rule: In the 14th century two brothers, Harihara and Bukka Raya, who had served as governors under Muhammad bin Tughlaq, rejected Delhi's authority and founded the kingdom that grew into the Vijayanagara Empire, with its capital at Hampi in present-day Karnataka. Its northern rival, the Bahmani Sultanate, fragmented into five Deccan Sultanates -- Bijapur, Golconda, Berar, Ahmednagar and Bidar -- each under a former governor or tarafdar; Vijayanagara also fought the Gajapati rulers of Odisha. The empire reached its peak in the 16th century under Krishnadevaraya, who patronised Sanskrit, Telugu and Kannada scholars, composed the Telugu epic Amuktamalyada with its Rajaniti section on good governance, and gave grants to temples including Tirupati and the Vitthala temple. He died of illness in 1529; in 1565 a coalition of Deccan Sultanates defeated Ramaraya at the Battle of Talikota, the capital was sacked over several months, and the empire fragmented under the Nayakas before ending in the mid-17th century.
concepts.example: The Portuguese traveller Domingo Paes wrote that the city 'seemed to me as large as Rome, and very beautiful to the sight'.

questions.q: Talikota was a single defeat, yet the empire never recovered from it. Explain why.
questions.a: What followed the defeat was the destruction of the capital itself over several months: houses, shops, palaces and most of the temples were ruined and much of the civilian population massacred, so the centre of government, trade and wealth was gone. With no capital and no ruler of Krishnadevaraya's stature, power passed to the Nayakas in the regions, and the empire ended in the mid-17th century.
s: The capital was destroyed, not just the army defeated
Loss of the centre of government, trade and wealth
Power passed to the Nayakas and the empire ended

questions.q: Do you think a ruler was right to spend the treasury on temples and poets, as Krishnadevaraya did? Give a reason.
questions.a: Opinions may vary; a reasoned answer is accepted, for example that such patronage produced lasting art, literature and pilgrim centres that also drew trade, or on the other hand that the same money could have strengthened the empire's defences.
s: Position stated
Reason drawn from the chapter

questions.q: Imagine you are a horse trader arriving at Vijayanagara. Write a short note home describing the city and the welcome you receive.
questions.a: A note mentioning the huge and beautiful city with its gardens, water channels and crowded markets full of laden oxen, and the unusually warm welcome, because the king wants the horses and does not want rival kingdoms to buy them.
s: Two accurate details about the city
The reason for the warm welcome
A coherent first-person note

concepts.name: The Mughals from Babur to Shah Jahan
concepts.description: Babur's victory at Panipat and the founding of the Mughal Empire, the Sur interlude under Humayun, Akbar's mixture of brutality and tolerance, and the art and architecture of Jahangir and Shah Jahan.
concepts.idea: The Mughal Empire was founded by conquest in 1526, nearly lost and regained, and then held together by Akbar with alliances and tolerance as much as with arms.
concepts.rule: Babur, a Turkic-Mongol ruler and a descendant of Timur who had been driven out of Samarkand, defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 using gunpowder, field artillery and matchlock guns; that ended the Delhi Sultanate and founded the Mughal Empire. His memoirs, the Baburnama, show him as both cultured and ruthless, and he stayed in India for its wealth. After his death in 1530 Humayun lost ground to Sher Shah Suri's Sur Empire before reconquering it; Himu then seized Delhi as Hemchandra Vikramaditya until Akbar defeated him at the Second Battle of Panipat. Akbar became emperor at 13 and reigned almost fifty years, from 1556 to 1605. His reign blended brutality, as at Chittor, with tolerance: marriage alliances, Rajput and regional leaders at court, the jizya abolished, sulh-i-kul or 'peace with all', and a house of translation at Fatehpur Sikri. Jahangir and Shah Jahan carried on the flowering of art and architecture, which produced the Taj Mahal, Humayun's tomb and the Red Forts of Delhi and Agra.
concepts.example: At his house of translation in Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar had the Mahabharata turned into Persian as the Razmnama, the 'Book of War'.

questions.a: Brutality: at Chittor he besieged the fort for over five months and then ordered the massacre of some 30,000 civilians, enslaving the surviving women and children. Tolerance: later he abolished the jizya, held interfaith dialogues and appointed Hindu officials to high posts.

questions.q: Explain how the Mughals lost and then regained control of north India between 1530 and 1556.
questions.a: After Babur died in 1530 his son Humayun could not hold the empire together, and Sher Shah Suri built the Sur Empire across large parts of north India. Humayun later reconquered the lost ground, but died in an accident. Meanwhile Himu, a wazir under one of the last Suri rulers, captured Delhi, until Babur's grandson Akbar defeated and beheaded him at the Second Battle of Panipat and reclaimed Delhi for the Mughals.

questions.a: A is true, R is false

questions.q: What does the practice of jauhar tell us about what the defenders of Chittor expected if the fort fell?
questions.a: They expected the women to be taken as slaves or abused by the victorious army, which is why hundreds went into mass fires instead; jauhar was regarded as a heroic act of final resistance and a way of preserving honour.

questions.q: The chapter quotes both Akbar's boastful victory message from Chittor and his later words of shame recorded by Abul Fazl. What do the two quotations together show?
questions.a: They show that his outlook changed across a long reign. At 25 he boasted of destroying temples and establishing Islam with a bloodthirsty sword; later he said he was overwhelmed with shame at having forced men into conformity, and asked what constancy could be expected from people converted under compulsion. Together they mark the move from force towards sulh-i-kul, and also remind us that a ruler's own words are a source a historian has to weigh.
s: The early boast
The later regret
What the change shows

questions.q: Babur's memoirs record his cruelty as well as his learning. Is such a candid source more useful to a historian than a flattering court chronicle? Give a reason.
questions.a: Opinions may vary; a reasoned answer is accepted, for example that a candid memoir is more trustworthy because the writer admits what does not flatter him, though it is still one man's version of events.

Reason given

questions.a: An entry naming, for example, the Taj Mahal at Agra, Humayun's tomb in Delhi and the Red Forts of Delhi and Agra, and mentioning miniature painting or calligraphy as another art form that flourished in the period.
s: Three buildings correctly named
Another art form named
Written as a catalogue entry

concepts.name: Aurangzeb and the strain on the Mughal Empire
concepts.description: Aurangzeb's violent accession, his religious policy and the reimposed taxes, the Deccan wars that drained the treasury, and how the chapter asks students to read a period of atrocities.
concepts.idea: Under Aurangzeb the Mughal Empire reached its greatest size and its greatest strain at once, and the cost of holding it explains the rapid decline after 1707.
concepts.rule: When Shah Jahan fell ill in 1657 he wanted the throne to pass to his eldest son Dara Shikoh, but Aurangzeb defeated and executed Dara, removed his other two brothers, imprisoned his father in the Agra Fort and crowned himself in 1658 as Alamgir, 'conqueror of the world'. He ruled almost 49 years. A skilled soldier, he pushed the empire to its greatest expansion while facing constant rebellion, and spent his last 25 years at war in the Deccan; maintaining those armies depleted the treasury and strained the administration, which is often held to be a key reason for the rapid decline of Mughal power after his death in 1707. Deeply religious and austere, he banned practices he regarded as un-Islamic such as music and dance at court, and reimposed both the jizya and a pilgrimage tax on Hindus, which Akbar had abolished. His 1669 farman ordered governors to demolish schools and temples of the 'infidels'; temples at Banaras, Mathura and Somnath, Jain temples and Sikh gurudwaras were destroyed, and he also persecuted Sufis and Zoroastrians.
concepts.example: The chapter notes that the average reign was about nine years for the Delhi sultans but 27 years for Mughal emperors up to Aurangzeb.

s: He was deeply religious and austere

He had one of his other two brothers arrested and executed and drove the second into exile. He then imprisoned Shah Jahan in the Agra Fort, where he stayed until his death, and crowned himself emperor in 1658.

The other two brothers removed

questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Referring to the note on history's darker chapters, explain what this chapter asks of a student who is reading about atrocities.
questions.a: It asks the student to learn the facts rather than look away from them, to give the victims respect and remembrance, and at the same time to remember that these were the acts of individuals hundreds of years ago, so that people living today bear no responsibility for them and should not be blamed for them.

questions.q: In his last letters Aurangzeb wrote, 'I have not done well for the country and the people'. What do you think those words tell us about him?
questions.a: Opinions may vary; a reasoned answer is accepted, for example that after 49 years of war he judged his own reign a failure and died without hope, which reads as genuine regret and contrasts sharply with the pride of his earlier edicts.
s: A reading of the words offered
A reason drawn from the chapter

questions.q: Write two headlines and a one-line summary for a news sheet of 1707 reporting Aurangzeb's death: one headline written at court and one written in the Deccan.
questions.a: A court headline stressing the passing of Alamgir after almost 49 years and the empire at its greatest extent; a Deccan headline stressing 25 years of unending war and an exhausted treasury; and a summary line that holds both truths together.
s: A court headline

concepts.name: Resistance to the Mughals: peasants, tribes, Rajputs and Ahoms
concepts.description: The Jat peasant rising, tribal resistance and Rani Durgavati, the surge of the Rajputs under Rana Sanga and Maharana Pratap, and the Ahom kingdom's paik system and victory at Saraighat.
concepts.idea: Mughal power was worn down from below and from the edges, by peasants, tribal groups, Rajput clans and the Ahoms, who used their own terrain and guerrilla tactics against far larger armies.
concepts.rule: Peasant communities rebelled against harsh exploitation: in the 17th century the Jat peasantry killed an oppressive Mughal officer and 20,000 of them fought the Mughal army before the rising was suppressed. Tribal groups such as the Bhils, Gonds, Santhals and Kochs resisted annexation and taxation, and those in forested, hilly or remote regions kept some independence; Rani Durgavati of the Garha kingdom kept 20,000 soldiers and 1,000 elephants and died on the battlefield in 1564 rather than be captured. The Rajputs rebuilt after the Khiljis' conquest into two major clans in Mewar and Marwar; Rana Sanga united several clans before losing to Babur at Khanwa, and Maharana Pratap, defeated at Haldighati in 1576, escaped and waged guerrilla warfare from the Aravallis with strong Bhil support, which the Mewar emblem records. Durga Das Rathore rebelled under Aurangzeb, and Mughal authority stayed limited in Rajasthan. The Ahoms, who migrated from present-day Myanmar in the 13th century, ran the paik system, in which every able-bodied man gave labour or military service for land rights, and at the Battle of Saraighat in 1671 Lachit Borphukan and 10,000 men defeated a Mughal force of 30,000.
concepts.example: Maharana Pratap's Bhil allies fought as archers and guided his troops through the Aravalli hills, which is why a Bhil warrior stands on the Mewar emblem.

questions.a: Although the Mughal army had the upper hand in 1576 he escaped, and for years afterwards he waged guerrilla warfare from the Aravalli hills, living in harsh conditions rather than accept Mughal suzerainty, so Mewar was never made to submit.

questions.q: How did the geography of Assam help the Ahoms defeat a much larger Mughal force?
questions.a: Dense forests, hills and rivers gave cover and made movement difficult for a big army, and the Ahoms knew the ground well enough to keep up guerrilla tactics; at Saraighat the fighting was on the Brahmaputra, which suited their skill with boats.

questions.a: Only II

questions.q: Describe the Jat rising of the 17th century and say what it shows about peasant resistance.
questions.a: The Jat peasantry of what is now western Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and eastern Rajasthan killed an oppressive officer of the Mughal administration, and in the battle that followed 20,000 of them confronted the Mughal army and fought valiantly, but their leader was killed and the rebellion was suppressed. It shows that harsh exploitation could drive ordinary cultivators into armed revolt in very large numbers, even though they could rarely defeat a trained imperial army.
s: The trigger and the killing of the officer
20,000 men, the leader killed and the rising suppressed
What it shows about peasant resistance

questions.q: The Mughal general Ram Singh praised Assamese soldiers as expert at rowing, archery, digging trenches and handling guns and cannon. Explain why such versatility mattered in a war in the Brahmaputra Valley.
questions.a: A campaign there had to be fought on water as much as on land, so men who could row and fight from boats were essential at Saraighat. Trenches gave defence in wet, forested country where a large army could not manoeuvre. Skill with both bows and firearms meant the same men could fight at any range without waiting for specialists. Together this let 10,000 Ahoms defeat 30,000 Mughals.

concepts.name: The rise of the Sikhs
concepts.description: Guru Nanak's teaching, the turn to martial defence under Guru Hargobind, the martyrdom of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the founding of the Khalsa, and the Sikh Empire of Maharaja Ranjit Singh.
concepts.idea: A purely spiritual movement in 15th century Punjab was pushed into armed self-defence by persecution, and ended as a centralised Sikh Empire holding the Northwest.
concepts.rule: In 15th century Punjab, Guru Nanak spread a message of equality, compassion and the oneness of God, Ik Onkar, and his followers became known as Sikhs. When Jahangir found that Guru Arjan had supported his rebellious son he had the Guru tortured to death, and Guru Arjan's son and successor Guru Hargobind introduced martial training and raised a Sikh army. The Guru Granth Sahib, first compiled by Guru Arjan with Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns added later, teaches one God for all and enjoins truthfulness, compassion, humility and self-control. In 1675 Kashmiri Pandits sought Guru Tegh Bahadur's protection from persecution; he stood with them, refused Aurangzeb's order to convert even under torture, and was publicly beheaded at Chandni Chowk in Delhi, where the Gurudwara Sis Ganj Sahib now stands. His son Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth and last Guru, founded the Khalsa, a martial brotherhood committed to justice, equality and defence of the faith. As Mughal power declined, Sikh confederacies emerged and were unified by Maharaja Ranjit Singh at the turn of the 19th century into a centralised Sikh Empire spanning much of the Northwest, including parts of Kashmir.
concepts.example: The Guru Granth Sahib teaches that 'Truth is high but higher still is truthful living'.

questions.q: Explain why the Sikh Empire belongs in a chapter about the reshaping of India's political map.
questions.a: As Mughal power collapsed, especially under Maratha pressure, Sikh confederacies filled the vacuum in the Punjab region, and Maharaja Ranjit Singh welded them into one strong centralised state spanning much of the Northwest, including parts of Kashmir. Until the middle of the 19th century that state held the region against both Mughal remnants and British expansion, so a region once governed from Delhi appears on the map as an independent power.
s: The vacuum left by Mughal decline
Ranjit Singh unifies the confederacies into a centralised state
A new independent power on the map, resisting Mughal remnants and the British

questions.q: The Sikh Regiment has saluted the Gurudwara Sis Ganj Sahib before the President in the Republic Day parade every year since 1979. Why do you think such a custom is kept up?
questions.a: Opinions may vary; a reasoned answer is accepted, for example that it keeps public memory of Guru Tegh Bahadur's sacrifice for another community's freedom of worship, which the chapter calls a powerful symbol of faith and sacrifice in Indian history.
s: An explanation offered

Why he was there and what he stood for
Written as a plaque addressed to a visitor

concepts.name: Administering India and people's lives
concepts.description: The iqta system and the sultan's council, Akbar's ministries, subahs and the mansabdari system, Todar Mal's revenue surveys, and the agriculture, crafts, trade, hundis and temple economies that supported ordinary life.
concepts.idea: Two very different administrative systems collected the revenue of a decentralised economy whose agriculture, crafts, trade networks and temple economies kept India among the wealthiest regions in the world.
concepts.rule: Under the Delhi Sultanate the sultan held absolute authority as political and military head, assisted by a council of ministers; the iqta system assigned territories to nobles called iqtadars who collected taxes and sent the surplus to the treasury, their posts loyal to the centre but not hereditary, with the burden falling hardest on the peasantry. Akbar reorganised the Mughal machinery: the Diwan for finances, the Mir Bakhshi for the military, the Khan-i-Saman for public works, trade, industry, agriculture and the royal household, and the Sadr for justice and religious and educational matters, with such ministers in each of the twelve subahs, checks and balances between officials, and village self-governance left largely undisturbed. Under the mansabdari system, recorded by Abul Fazl in the Ain-i-Akbari, mansabdars kept a set number of troops and animals for their rank and were paid with land called jagirs. Todar Mal's surveys of crop yields, prices and land boosted revenue. The economy rested on agriculture taxed at about one-fifth of the produce, on crafts and ship-building, on exports through ports such as Calicut, Surat and Hooghly, on hundis and merchant credit, and on temples that ran markets, infrastructure and lending.
concepts.example: A hundi was a written instruction to pay a named person, so a merchant could move money across political boundaries without carrying coin.

questions.q: Why did the hundi system make merchants less vulnerable to plunder?
questions.a: A hundi was only a written instruction to pay, so funds could be moved across political boundaries without anyone carrying actual coin along the road, which left nothing valuable for robbers or armies to seize.
s: No currency was physically carried
Nothing valuable to seize, so money moved safely across borders

questions.q: How did the mansabdari system let Akbar assemble an army at short notice without keeping a permanent central army?
questions.a: Every mansabdar had to maintain, according to his rank, a precise number of troops along with elephants, horses and camels for the state, and regular inspections checked that he had done so, so the emperor could call those contingents in whenever he needed an army.
s: Each rank had to keep a set number of troops and animals ready
Inspections ensured readiness, so forces could be summoned quickly

questions.q: Explain two ways in which temples acted as economic institutions and not only as places of worship.
questions.a: Land and wealth donated to them as dana was used by temple managers to build community infrastructure such as irrigation works and tanks and to run pilgrim accommodation such as dharmashalas and chhatrams; temples also gave merchants credit and funded internal and maritime trade, and bustling markets grew up around them.
s: Infrastructure and pilgrim accommodation funded from dana
Credit for merchants and funding for trade

questions.q: Consider: (I) Under Akbar the share of non-Muslim officials in the higher ranks of the administration rarely exceeded one-third. (II) At the village level, traditional structures of self-governance continued more or less undisturbed. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Both I and II

questions.q: Explain why the late 1600s brought economic stress to peasants even though India was still a land of abundance.
questions.a: After land revenue and payments to intermediary parties, peasants were often left with only a small share of their own produce, so many lost their land and became bonded labourers; craftspeople and labourers also faced harsh conditions, and frequent warfare displaced whole populations. India's wealth was real, as Arab and European travellers testified, but it was concentrated in the hands of rulers, courtiers, high officials and the merchant class, so abundance and hardship existed side by side.
s: Taxes and intermediaries left the peasant very little
Loss of land, bonded labour and displacement by war
Wealth concentrated in a few hands

questions.q: Give one way in which the iqta system and the mansabdari system were alike and one way in which they differed.
questions.a: Both paid officers by assigning them the revenue of land rather than cash from a central treasury. They differed in what was demanded in return: an iqtadar mainly collected taxes and sent the surplus to the sultan's treasury, while a mansabdar had to maintain a fixed number of troops and animals for his rank and was regularly inspected.
s: One similarity
One difference

questions.q: Trader communities such as the Marwaris built parallel systems of credit and trust that worked without the ruling classes. Explain why such systems were so valuable in a period of frequent political change.
questions.a: Dynasties rose and fell and boundaries moved constantly, so a merchant who depended on one ruler's protection could lose everything when that ruler fell. A network built on hundis and on trust between trading families worked under any regime, moved money without carrying coin that could be plundered, and did not need the participation of the ruling classes at all, so trade and credit survived wars and changes of government.
s: Political instability made official protection unreliable
Hundis and trust networks worked across regimes and avoided carrying coin
Trade and credit therefore survived the changes

questions.q: Which do you think did more to strengthen Akbar's state: Todar Mal's revenue surveys or the mansabdari system? Give a reason.
questions.a: Opinions may vary; a reasoned answer is accepted, for example that the surveys of crop yields, prices and land boosted collection and so paid for everything else, or that the mansabdari system supplied the army that actually held the empire together.
s: Position stated
Reason drawn from the chapter

questions.a: Exports such as cotton textiles, spices and craft goods like utensils, ornaments or jewellery; imports such as horses, metals or luxury goods; and a line noting that India produced most of what it needed, so it bought mainly what it lacked, such as horses.

Two imports listed
The explanatory line
